title: Kohler's Rule Holds in the Strange Metallic Hubbard Model
authors: Rebekah M. Jin, Emily Z. Zhang, Jixun K. Ding, Brian Moritz, Thomas P. Devereaux
abstract: Unconventional magnetotransport violating Kohler's rule has been reported in many strongly correlated strange metals, but the exact origin of these violations is yet unknown. To investigate this question, we use determinant quantum Monte Carlo to compute the magnetoresistance of the hole-doped Hubbard-Hofstadter model. Despite $T$-linear resistivity exceeding the Mott-Ioffe-Regel limit and the nominal absence of well-defined quasiparticles, we find Kohler's rule unexpectedly holds across a wide range of on-site interaction strengths and hole dopings. In particular, Kohler emerges below a crossover temperature $T^\star\approx t$ identified from the double occupancy and specific heat, coinciding with the onset of local singlet correlations between lattice sites. We thus propose that Kohler scaling in this regime reflects a more general form of many-body quantum coherence. Our results show that strong correlations and strange metallicity do not themselves generically produce anomalous magnetoresistance.
summary: This theoretical study uses Quantum Monte Carlo simulations on the Hubbard-Hofstadter model to investigate magnetotransport in strange metals. Despite the system exhibiting hallmarks of non-Fermi liquid behavior, the authors demonstrate that Kohler's rule for magnetoresistance surprisingly holds. This suggests that the underlying physics is governed by a robust many-body quantum coherence mechanism.
main_problem: The study investigates the origin of anomalous magnetotransport in strange metals, specifically testing whether Kohler's rule holds despite strong correlations and the breakdown of conventional quasiparticle descriptions.
main_result: The authors find that Kohler's rule unexpectedly holds in the strongly correlated Hubbard-Hofstadter model, suggesting that the scaling reflects a general form of many-body quantum coherence rather than quasiparticle behavior.
method: The research employs Determinant Quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) simulations combined with advanced analytic continuation techniques (like Constrained MaxEnt) to extract real-frequency transport coefficients from imaginary-time correlation functions.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the hole-doped Hubbard-Hofstadter model, a minimal lattice Hamiltonian used to simulate interacting electrons in a magnetic field. The calculations are performed on finite lattices ($8 	imes 8$ or $10 	imes 10$).
key_observables: Magnetoresistance (MR), longitudinal resistivity ($ho_{xx}$), transverse conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$), double occupancy ($\langle d angle$), and specific heat ($c_V$).
important_parameters: Strong on-site interaction ($U/t$), hole doping ($\langle n angle$), and temperature ($T/t$). A key crossover temperature is $T^\star \approx t$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the DQMC method, coupled with constrained MaxEnt, can accurately map imaginary-time correlation functions to real-frequency transport spectra.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature dependence of $\langle d angle$ and $c_V$ showing extrema at $T^\star/t \approx 1$, and show Kohler plots demonstrating the collapse of MR data onto a universal scaling function below a characteristic field $B^\star$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using the Hubbard-Hofstadter model and DQMC. It then details the complex numerical methods for extracting real-frequency conductivities. The core analysis focuses on calculating and plotting the magnetoresistance across various doping and interaction regimes, culminating in the confirmation of Kohler's scaling law.
why_interesting: The finding that a simple scaling law like Kohler's rule persists in a regime characterized by strong correlations and non-Fermi liquid behavior is highly relevant to understanding emergent quantum phenomena in strongly correlated materials.
